entries.input: Let $k$ be a nonnegative integer. Prove that $\sum_{j=0}^{k} 2^{k-j} \binom{k+j}{j} = 4^{k}$.
entries.name: Putnam2020A2
entries.conclusion: ∑ j ∈ Finset.range (k + 1), 2 ^ (k - j) * Nat.choose (k + j) j = 4 ^ k
entries.title: Putnam 2020 A2

entries.input: Let $k$ be a nonnegative integer. Prove that $\sum_{j=0}^{k-1} 2^{k-j} \binom{k+j}{j} = 4^{k}$.
entries.name: Putnam2020A2Twin
entries.conclusion: ∑ j ∈ Finset.range k, 2 ^ (k - j) * Nat.choose (k + j) j = 4 ^ k
entries.title: Putnam 2020 A2, top term dropped
entries.rationale: A soundness twin for `putnam-2020-a2`: the sum stops one term short, dropping $\binom{2k}{k}$. The identity then fails for every $k$ -- at $k = 1$ the left side is $2$ and the right is $4$ -- but an off-by-one in a summation bound is the error a model is likeliest to wave through, which is what this measures. It states nothing the paper asked, so it cites no occurrence.

entries.input: Let $n \geq 2$. For a sequence $s = (s_1, \dots, s_{n-1})$ with each $s_i = \pm 1$, let $f(s)$ be the number of permutations $(a_1, \dots, a_n)$ of $\{1, \dots, n\}$ with $s_i(a_{i+1} - a_i) > 0$ for every $i$. Prove that $f(s)$ is largest exactly when $s$ is one of the two alternating sequences, $s_i = (-1)^{i}$ and $s_i = (-1)^{i+1}$.
entries.name: Putnam2025A5
entries.binders: (n : ℕ) (hn : 2 ≤ n) (f : (ℕ → ℤ) → ℕ) (hf : ∀ t : ℕ → ℤ, f t = Nat.card {a : Equiv.Perm (Fin n) // ∀ i j : Fin n, (j : ℕ) = (i : ℕ) + 1 → 0 < t (i : ℕ) * (((a j : Fin n) : ℕ) - ((a i : Fin n) : ℕ) : ℤ)}) (s : ℕ → ℤ) (hs : ∀ i, i + 1 < n → (s i = 1 ∨ s i = -1))
entries.title: Putnam 2025 A5
entries.witness_note: `f` is pinned to an `n`-dependent cardinality by `hf`, so closing the binders under `∃` means writing that whole expression again at a fixed `n`. Recorded as a debt rather than guessed.

entries.input: Let $n$ and $k$ be positive integers, and fill the square in row $i$ and column $j$ of an $n \times n$ grid with $i + j - k$. Prove that one can choose $n$ squares, no two in the same row or column, whose entries are exactly $1, 2, \dots, n$ if and only if $n$ is odd and $k = (n+1)/2$.
entries.name: Putnam2024B1
entries.conclusion: (∃ σ : Equiv.Perm (Fin n), ∀ m : ℤ, (1 ≤ m ∧ m ≤ (n : ℤ)) ↔ ∃ i : Fin n, (((i : ℕ) : ℤ) + 1) + (((σ i : Fin n) : ℕ) : ℤ) + 1 - (k : ℤ) = m) ↔ (Odd n ∧ 2 * k = n + 1)
entries.title: Putnam 2024 B1
